title: Countability and the Uncountability of R: Examples and Counterexamples

items.title: The integers are countably infinite: $\mathbb{Z} \approx \mathbb{N}$
items.statement: $\mathbb{Z} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the integers are countably infinite ([[def-countable]]). The argument is the two-injection route of [[thm-schroder-bernstein]] rather than a closed formula. The embedding $\iota(n) = [(n,0)]$ is injective ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and the quotient map $\pi(a,b) = [(a,b)]$ is a surjective function $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ ([[thm-universal-property-of-the-quotient]], [[def-integers]]); composing $\pi$ with the bijection $\beta$ of [[thm-n-cross-n-countable]] exhibits $\mathbb{Z}$ as a surjective image of $\mathbb{N}$, and [[lem-countable-iff-surjection-from-n]] then supplies an injection $\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{N}$ explicitly as $j(x) = \min\{\, k \in \mathbb{N} : \pi(\beta(k)) = x \,\}$. Every ingredient is a definition or a canonical least element, so no choice principle is used; [[thm-product-of-countable]] then gives that $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}$ is at most countable as well.
items.strategy: Two injections, then Schröder-Bernstein. (1) $\mathbb{N} \preceq \mathbb{Z}$: $\iota(n) = [(n,0)]$ is injective by [[lem-nat-embeds-int]]. (2) $\mathbb{Z} \preceq \mathbb{N}$: the quotient map of the equivalence relation on $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ that defines $\mathbb{Z}$ ([[def-integers]], well defined by [[lem-int-equivalence]]) is a surjective function ([[thm-universal-property-of-the-quotient]]); composing with $\beta$ gives a surjection $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ with $\mathbb{Z} \ne \varnothing$, so [[lem-countable-iff-surjection-from-n]] produces an injection by the least-index rule, with no selection. (3) [[thm-schroder-bernstein]] converts the pair of injections into a bijection. (4) The product theorem gives $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}$ at most countable.

items.title: Deleting one point of a countably infinite set leaves a set equinumerous with it
items.statement: Let $X$ be countably infinite ([[def-countable]]) and let $x \in X$. Then $X \approx X \setminus \{x\}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): deleting one point leaves a set of the same size, and $X \setminus \{x\}$ is a proper subset of $X$ ([[def-set-difference-and-symmetric-difference]], [[def-subset-and-proper-subset]]). The basic instance is $X = \mathbb{N}$, $x = 0$, where the witness is the successor map $\sigma$, a bijection $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \setminus \{0\}$ ([[thm-omega-is-peano-system]], [[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); a general $X$ transports a shift of $\mathbb{N}$ along a bijection $\mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[thm-a-function-is-a-bijection-exactly-when-it-has-a-two-sided-inverse]], [[prop-composition-preserves-injectivity-surjectivity-and-bijectivity]]). No finite set shares the behaviour: by claim 5 of [[lem-pigeonhole]] no finite set is equinumerous with a proper subset of itself. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: (1) For each $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $\varphi_n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \setminus \{n\}$ by $\varphi_n(k) = k$ for $k < n$ and $\varphi_n(k) = \sigma(k)$ for $k \ge n$. Trichotomy makes it a function; $\sigma$ injective and $\sigma(k) > k$ make it injective; and it is onto: for $m < n$ take $k = m$, and for $m > n$ write $m = \sigma(j)$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]) with $n \le j$ by discreteness ([[lem-nat-discrete]]), so $\varphi_n(j) = m$. (2) For countably infinite $X$ fix a bijection $e : \mathbb{N} \to X$ and $x = e(n)$; then $e \circ \varphi_n \circ e^{-1}$ is a bijection from $X$ onto $X \setminus \{x\}$, whose image is $e[\mathbb{N} \setminus \{n\}] = X \setminus \{x\}$, the image computed from injectivity of $e$. (3) Contrast: if a finite $F$ had a proper subset $A$ with $F \approx A$, transporting along a bijection $F \to m$ would give $m \approx \varphi^{-1}[A]$ with $\varphi^{-1}[A]$ a proper subset of $m$, contradicting claim 5 of [[lem-pigeonhole]].

items.title: $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ is uncountable
items.statement: The power set $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ is uncountable ([[def-countable]]): there is no surjection $\mathbb{N} \to \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ ([[thm-cantor-powerset]]), so $\mathbb{N} \prec \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ ([[def-equinumerous]]). The proof combines Cantor's theorem with [[thm-schroder-bernstein]]: the map $n \mapsto \{n\}$ is injective ([[def-unordered-pair-and-singleton]], [[lem-unordered-pair-equality]]), so $\mathbb{N} \preceq \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$; if $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ were at most countable, that is $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N}) \preceq \mathbb{N}$, Schröder-Bernstein would give a bijection $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N}) \to \mathbb{N}$ and hence a surjection $\mathbb{N} \to \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$, contradicting Cantor's theorem. No choice principle is used. This is [[thm-cantor-powerset]], in the 'strictly larger' form $\mathbb{N} \prec \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$, instantiated at $\mathbb{N}$.
items.strategy: (1) $\mathbb{N} \preceq \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$: $n \mapsto \{n\}$ is injective, since $\{n\} = \{m\}$ forces $n = m$ by [[lem-unordered-pair-equality]]. (2) If $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ is finite, say $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N}) \approx n$, then composing a bijection with the inclusion $n \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]], [[def-subset-and-proper-subset]]) gives $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N}) \preceq \mathbb{N}$; if it is countably infinite this is immediate. (3) [[thm-schroder-bernstein]] then yields $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N}) \approx \mathbb{N}$, and a bijection is a surjection, contradicting [[thm-cantor-powerset]]. Hence $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ is not at most countable.

items.title: The set of binary sequences is equinumerous with $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$, hence uncountable
items.statement: Let $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ be the set of all functions $\mathbb{N} \to \{0,1\}$, where $0 = \varnothing$ and $1 = \sigma(0)$ ([[def-the-set-of-functions-from-one-set-to-another]], [[def-unordered-pair-and-singleton]]). The map $S \mapsto \chi_S$ sending $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ to its characteristic function, $\chi_S(n) = 1$ for $n \in S$ and $\chi_S(n) = 0$ for $n \notin S$, is a bijection $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N}) \to \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). Hence $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} \approx \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ ([[def-equinumerous]]) and the set of binary sequences is uncountable ([[ex-power-set-of-the-naturals-is-uncountable]]). This is the function-space form of Cantor's diagonal argument, and it is the form in which the library records that infinite products of at-most-countable sets need not be at most countable. No choice principle is used.
items.strategy: (1) For $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ form $\chi_S := \{(n,v) \in \mathbb{N} \times \{0,1\} : (n \in S \wedge v = 1) \vee (n \notin S \wedge v = 0)\}$ by Separation; since $0 \ne 1$ ([[thm-omega-is-peano-system]]) exactly one value $v$ is related to each $n$, so $\chi_S$ is a function with domain $\mathbb{N}$ and values in $\{0,1\}$ ([[def-function]], [[def-cartesian-product]]). (2) Injectivity: if $\chi_S = \chi_T$ then $n \in S \iff \chi_S(n) = 1 \iff \chi_T(n) = 1 \iff n \in T$, so $S = T$ by Extensionality. (3) Surjectivity: for $f : \mathbb{N} \to \{0,1\}$ put $S := \{n : f(n) = 1\}$; each $f(n)$ is $1$ or $0$, and in the two cases $\chi_S(n) = 1 = f(n)$ or $\chi_S(n) = 0 = f(n)$, so $\chi_S = f$. (4) Uncountability transfers along the bijection: if $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ were at most countable, composing with the bijection would make $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ at most countable, contradicting [[ex-power-set-of-the-naturals-is-uncountable]].

items.title: The rationals in an interval are countably infinite while the interval is uncountable
items.statement:
Let $\mathbb{R}$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), let $\iota : \mathbb{Q} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the canonical embedding and write $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}} = \iota[\mathbb{Q}]$ ([[lem-of-q-embeds]]). For $a < b$ in $\mathbb{R}$ put $S_{a,b} = \{\, x \in \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}} : a < x < b \,\}$ and $I_{a,b} = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : a < x < b \,\}$. Then

- **(i)** $S_{a,b} \approx \mathbb{N}$: the rationals of any nondegenerate interval are countably infinite ([[def-countable]], [[def-equinumerous]]);
- **(ii)** $I_{a,b} \setminus \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is uncountable, although $S_{a,b}$ is an at most countable subset of $I_{a,b}$ that is dense in it ([[lem-of-q-dense]]) and $I_{a,b}$ itself is uncountable ([[cor-interval-uncountable]]).

Cardinality and order-density are independent properties of a subset of $\mathbb{R}$. Both parts are theorems of ZF: the enumeration in (i) is built by a canonical least-index recursion, and (ii) interleaves two given enumerations.
items.strategy: Part (i). (a) $S_{a,b} \subseteq \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}} \approx \mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[lem-of-q-embeds]], [[thm-rationals-countable]]), so $S_{a,b}$ is at most countable ([[lem-subset-of-countable]]). (b) Fix a bijection $e : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ (inverse of a bijection, [[thm-a-function-is-a-bijection-exactly-when-it-has-a-two-sided-inverse]]). For $x \in I_{a,b}$ let $k(x)$ be the least $k$ with $x < e(k) < b$; the set is nonempty because $\mathbb{R}$ is Archimedean ([[thm-of-archimedean]], [[def-archimedean-field]]) and the rationals are dense ([[lem-of-q-dense]]), and it has a least element ([[thm-well-ordering-principle]]). Put $F(x) = e(k(x)) \in (x,b)$. Recursion ([[thm-recursion]]) from the seed $r_0 = e(\min\{k : a < e(k) < b\})$ produces $r_{n+1} = F(r_n)$, so $r_0 < r_1 < \cdots$ and $n \mapsto r_n$ is an injection $\mathbb{N} \to S_{a,b}$; Schröder-Bernstein with (a) gives $S_{a,b} \approx \mathbb{N}$. Part (ii). Suppose $C := I_{a,b} \setminus \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ were at most countable. If $C = \varnothing$ then $I_{a,b} = S_{a,b}$ is at most countable; otherwise fix surjections $f, g : \mathbb{N} \to S_{a,b}, C$ ([[lem-countable-iff-surjection-from-n]]) and define $t : \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to I_{a,b}$ by $t(0,k) = f(k)$ and $t(n,k) = g(k)$ for $n \ne 0$; every point of $I_{a,b}$ lies in $S_{a,b}$ or in $C$, so $t$ is surjective, and composing with the bijection $\beta : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ ([[thm-n-cross-n-countable]]) makes $I_{a,b}$ at most countable, contradicting [[cor-interval-uncountable]]. The two enumerations are given, so no choice is spent.

items.title: The complement of an at most countable set of reals is uncountable
items.statement: Let $C \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be at most countable ([[def-countable]]). Then $\mathbb{R} \setminus C$ is uncountable. In particular deleting finitely many reals, or all rationals, leaves an uncountable set ([[cor-irrationals-uncountable]]), even though the deleted set may be dense ([[lem-of-q-dense]]). The proof is the two-set union argument and spends no choice principle — in contrast to [[thm-countable-union-of-countable]], which assumes $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for countable families.
items.strategy:
Suppose $\mathbb{R} \setminus C$ were at most countable. Write $\mathbb{R} = C \cup (\mathbb{R} \setminus C)$ by Extensionality: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ either $x \in C$ or $x 
otin C$ ([[def-subset-and-proper-subset]], [[def-set-difference-and-symmetric-difference]]). If one of the two sets is empty, $\mathbb{R}$ equals the other and is at most countable; if both are nonempty, [[lem-countable-iff-surjection-from-n]] gives surjections $f, g : \mathbb{N} 	o C$, $\mathbb{R} \setminus C$, and the map $t : \mathbb{N} 	imes \mathbb{N} 	o \mathbb{R}$ with $t(0,k) = f(k)$ and $t(n,k) = g(k)$ for $n 
e 0$ is surjective; composing with the bijection $ eta : \mathbb{N} 	o \mathbb{N} 	imes \mathbb{N}$ ([[thm-n-cross-n-countable]]) gives a surjection $\mathbb{N} 	o \mathbb{R}$, so $\mathbb{R}$ is at most countable by the criterion, since $\mathbb{R} 
e \varnothing$. Either way [[thm-r-uncountable]] is contradicted. Only two existential instantiations of given maps occur, so no choice principle is used.

items.title: A nonempty surjective image of $\mathbb{N}$ need not be equinumerous with $\mathbb{N}$
items.statement:
**Refuted claim:** if $A \ne \varnothing$ and there is a surjection $\mathbb{N} \to A$, then $A \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[lem-countable-iff-surjection-from-n]]).

The witness is $A = \sigma(0) = \{0\} = 1$, the one-element set of the von Neumann naturals, with the constant map $c : \mathbb{N} \to A$, $c(n) = 0$ ([[def-natural-numbers]], [[def-unordered-pair-and-singleton]], [[def-function]]). The map $c$ is surjective because $0 \in A$, and $A$ is at most countable because it is finite: the identity is a bijection $A \to \sigma(0)$; but $A \not\approx \mathbb{N}$, since $\mathbb{N}$ is equinumerous with no natural number ([[lem-pigeonhole]], claim 4). So a nonempty at most countable set need not be countably infinite: the enumeration a surjection provides may repeat values, and here it must ([[def-countable]], [[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).
items.strategy:
(1) $A = \sigma(0)$ is nonempty and $c = \mathbb{N} 	imes \{0\}$ is a function with domain $\mathbb{N}$ and values in $A$ ([[def-cartesian-product]]); it is surjective because its only value $0$ lies in $A$, and it is not injective because $0 
e \sigma(0)$ ([[thm-omega-is-peano-system]]). (2) $A \approx \sigma(0)$ via the identity, so $A$ is finite and hence at most countable. (3) $A 
ot\approx \mathbb{N}$: claim 4 of [[lem-pigeonhole]] states $\mathbb{N} 
ot\approx n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, and a bijection $A 	o \mathbb{N}$ together with $A \approx 1$ would give $\mathbb{N} \approx 1$ by transitivity of $\approx$ ([[def-equinumerous]]). Hence the refuted claim fails.

items.title: The empty set is at most countable but no function from $\mathbb{N}$ is onto it
items.statement:
**Refuted claim:** every at most countable set is a surjective image of $\mathbb{N}$.

The witness is $\varnothing$, which is finite, hence at most countable ([[def-countable]]); but there is no function $\mathbb{N} \to \varnothing$ at all ([[def-function]]). So the hypothesis $A \ne \varnothing$ cannot be dropped from the forward direction of [[lem-countable-iff-surjection-from-n]]: $\varnothing$ is at most countable, yet it has no surjection from $\mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]], [[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).
items.strategy: $\varnothing \approx 0$ via the empty function, so $\varnothing$ is finite and at most countable. If $f : \mathbb{N} \to \varnothing$ were a function then its domain would be $\mathbb{N}$ while $f \subseteq \mathbb{N} \times \varnothing = \varnothing$ ([[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-relation-domain-range-and-field]]), so $f = \varnothing$ and $\operatorname{dom} f = \varnothing \ne \mathbb{N}$; equivalently, $f(0)$ would have to be an element of $\varnothing$. Hence no surjection $\mathbb{N} \to \varnothing$ exists and the refuted claim fails.

references.title: John K. Hunter, An Introduction to Real Analysis (complete author-hosted lecture notes, 307 pp.)

items.title: An explicit enumeration of the rationals, with repetitions and then without them
items.statement: With N indexed from 0, put J(a,b)=2^a(2b+1)-1, the published bijection N^2 -> N. For n, uniquely decode (u,c)=J^{-1}(n) and (a,b)=J^{-1}(u). Let z(u)=[(a,b)] in the difference-pair construction of Z and let iota_N: N -> Z be the canonical embedding. Define q(n)=[(z(u),iota_N(c+1))] in Q. This is a completely specified surjection N -> Q, with q(0)=0, q(1)=1, q(2)=0, q(3)=-1. Its least-first-occurrence subsequence is a bijection N -> Q. No lowest-terms convention, gcd, infinite-family choice or unspecified enumeration is used.
items.strategy: Use precisely J=successor^{-1} composed with the J of thm-n-cross-n-countable; its inverse exists and is unique because that item proves bijectivity. Every integer is represented by a difference pair, hence z is onto Z; this is a specified map, not the bijection asserted by the original integers example. The denominator iota_N(c+1) is positive by lem-nat-embeds-int and successor positivity, so each rational class q(n) is defined. For any rational x choose one positive-denominator representative (p,v) by lem-rat-positive-denominator. Because v>0, lem-nat-embeds-int gives v=iota_N(k) with k>0; lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor gives k=c+1. Represent p=[(a,b)], set u=J(a,b) and n=J(u,c); then q(n)=x. This proves surjectivity without choosing representatives simultaneously. For a literal repetition-free enumeration, take t_0=0 and t_{j+1}=min{n : q(n) is not among q(t_0),...,q(t_j)}. Prove the set is nonempty: Q has the injective copy of N supplied by the integer/rational embeddings, so if q took only these finitely many values, an injection N into a finite set would contradict lem-pigeonhole claim4 (restriction to the successor of its cardinal gives claim1). This finite history recursion is a single self-map on finite lists, formed by Separation/Replacement and thm-recursion. Inductively t_j is increasing and all omitted earlier q-values have already appeared. To prove onto, fix n: if q(n) never appeared then every next least new index would be <=n, providing n+2 distinct indices in {0,...,n}, contrary to lem-pigeonhole. Thus j -> q(t_j) is both injective and onto. Preserve distinction between the quotient-class rational and its later embedded real value.

items.title: A real coefficient list of degree d has at most d real roots
items.statement: Let d be a natural number and let a_0,...,a_d be real numbers with a_d != 0. Using the finite sum and natural powers already defined on roots-and-rational-powers, put P(x)=sum_{k=0}^d a_k x^k, for every real x. Its real zero set is finite of cardinality at most d (including d=0, when it is empty). This is a statement about finite coefficient lists and their evaluations, requiring neither a polynomial-ring construction nor any choice axiom. It is a local prerequisite for the same-page algebraic-number example only.
items.strategy: Strong induction on d. For d=0, P(x)=a_0 !=0. For d>=1, if P has no real zero, finish; otherwise instantiate one r with P(r)=0 (one existential instantiation, not a choice family). Define b_{d-1}=a_d and, descending finitely for k=d-1,...,1, b_{k-1}=a_k+r*b_k; define Q(x)=sum_{k=0}^{d-1} b_k x^k. Finite distributivity and the recursion for powers/sums give (x-r)Q(x): coefficient of x^d is a_d, coefficient of x^k for 1<=k<=d-1 is b_{k-1}-r*b_k=a_k, and its constant is -r*b_0. Expanding the finite recurrence for b_0 gives r*b_0=sum_{k=1}^d a_k*r^k, so -r*b_0=a_0 by P(r)=0; this also works at r=0 since no division by r is used. Consequently P(x)=(x-r)Q(x) for all real x, proved entirely locally. The leading coefficient of Q is a_d !=0, so induction makes its real root set finite with cardinality <=d-1. Every root x of P other than r is a root of Q by lem-of-no-zero-divisors and x-r !=0. Thus the root set of P is contained in {r} union roots(Q), a finite set of size at most d. Supply the finite counting detail: if roots(Q) is listed by a bijection from m<=d-1, append r if not already listed; any subset of that list is indexed by a subset of m+1, which has a finite increasing enumeration by least-index recursion, with length <=m+1 by lem-pigeonhole. This proves actual finiteness and its quantitative bound, rather than inferring it from countability. Only field axioms, finite algebra, induction, and the finite-counting facts are consumed.

items.title: Real algebraic numbers are countably infinite, without choice
items.statement: Here algebraic numbers means the REAL set A={x in R : sum_{k=0}^d iota_Z(a_k)x^k=0 for some d in N and integer coefficient list a_0,...,a_d with a_d !=0}, where iota_Z is Z -> Q -> R. A is countably infinite in ZF. An injection A -> N is specified by the least code of an integer coefficient list having x as a root, paired with the rank of x in its finite increasing real-root list. All embedded rationals lie in A, and R minus A is uncountable. No claim about algebraic closure or complex algebraic numbers is made: the available ambient field is R.
items.strategy: Reuse the explicitly specified surjection z:N->Z in ex-explicit-enumeration-of-the-rationals and the published J:N^2->N. Decode each n uniquely as J(d,t_0). For k=0,...,d decode t_k=J(u_k,t_{k+1}) and put a_k=z(u_k); evaluate the embedded-real coefficient list if a_d!=0, and otherwise use the constant list (1), which has no roots. This defines EVERY code, without partial decoding. Every nonzero finite integer coefficient list with last entry nonzero occurs: choose each u_k canonically as min{u:z(u)=a_k}, take tail t_{d+1}=0, encode backwards t_k=J(u_k,t_{k+1}), and use n=J(d,t_0). Finite backwards recursion has no arbitrary-index choice. By the local root-bound lemma each coded list has a finite root set of cardinality at most d. A finite subset of the ordered real field has a unique increasing root listing: its least element exists by lem-finite-subsets-listable (minimum consequence), and repeated deletion defines the rest; finite counting proves termination. This unique listing is specified from the root set, so forming all listings is Replacement by unique definition, NOT countable choice. For x in A let n(x)=min{n:x is a root of coded list n}, and let j(x) be its zero-based position in that list. Then x -> J(n(x),j(x)) is injective since equal pairs identify one entry in one uniquely ordered root list. Its image is a subset of N, hence at most countable by lem-subset-of-countable; the bijection onto its image transfers countability to A. A contains the embedded Q: if rational q has representative p/v with v!=0 then the nonzero coefficient list (-p,v) evaluates to zero at its embedded value by the rational/real field embedding laws. Thus the canonical injection N -> Q -> R lands in A. Combine that injection with A -> N using thm-schroder-bernstein, giving A approximately N, not just countable. Finally, if R minus A were countable, take the explicit bijection N -> A supplied by Schroder-Bernstein and one surjection N -> (R minus A) (handle the empty case separately), interleave on N^2 by the first coordinate 0 versus nonzero, then compose J inverse. This would make R countable, contradicting thm-r-uncountable. Only two existentially given enumerations are used, no countable-family choice or general countable-union theorem. The new example describes algebraicity locally from coefficient lists and does not consume later def-algebraic-element or polynomial-ring suppliers.

items.title: Cantor diagonal construction misses every prescribed list of binary sequences
items.statement: Given any function s:N -> {0,1}^N, write s_n=s(n) and define d:N -> {0,1} by d(n)=1 if s_n(n)=0 and d(n)=0 if s_n(n)=1. Then d differs from s_n at coordinate n for every n, so d is outside the range of s. In particular no prescribed list of binary sequences is onto. This is a direct choice-free diagonal construction, not a decimal expansion argument; no sum, limit or real digit convention is required.
items.strategy: Form the graph of d by Separation from N x {0,1}, using (n,1) iff s(n)(n)=0 and (n,0) iff s(n)(n)=1. Because s(n) is a function on N and 0 differs from 1, exactly one of these values occurs for every n, so this graph is a function N->{0,1}. For each n, either s_n(n)=0, making d(n)=1 !=s_n(n), or s_n(n)=1, making d(n)=0 !=s_n(n). Equality of functions would force equality at coordinate n, hence d != s_n for all n and s is not onto. The function space is a set by the earlier proved function-set supplier. If it were at most countable, it is nonempty (constant0 exists) and lem-countable-iff-surjection-from-n would supply such an onto s, contradiction. This verifies uncountability directly and agrees with the earlier characteristic-function bijection example. Every diagonal entry and its complementary value is uniquely defined; no choice axiom is used.
